items.title: William Russell Interview, 1962-09-04
items.q: had played in Audubon Park along with Ori and Bud Scott and Mutt

ctx.x: What kind of music do you think they were playing? Would it differ in any way from say what they were playing in the middle 20s?

I would doubt it myself just from the evidence of people's styles not changing that rapidly. I can't, we don't have any records of them. Actually the original Dixieland was the first to record. It might have been of course they always called it ragtime. A lot has been made like for instance in Brun's book on Nick LaRocca always made a big point of that. That they were the first ones to use the word jazz. But not, I'm not trying to say the colored people were first or anything of that kind in this particular case…

You were talking about... Yeah, a lot of the Negroes down here, they're all crazy about him. They all try to imitate him. And yet occasionally you run across some of the old timers that'll say, well, he plays novelty music. It's not really good jazz. Of course, all the young record collectors, and especially, say the ones...

items.q: That was the greatest rhythm section I ever heard, I'd say, was that Kid Ori rhythm section

ctx.x: Now these are typed in the back of the Defender notes.

Yeah. That's some of the later Defender notes, some things that I probably didn't get. He probably looked through my notes and then went up there and went through a couple of years. We'll copy all this stuff for you. So in any case, there are a few other interviews, people that are dead there like Tubby Hall and Joe Lindsay. Unfortunately, we got very little bit from Tubby Hall. I wanted to apologize on that. He was one of the great drummers, I'm convinced the more I hear of other drummers especially. At that…

items.title: William Russell Interview, 1976-02-16
items.q: I did, uh, record that Roy Palmer I got on trombone and later Kid Ory on trombone. And, uh, um, St. Cyr, of course, and Pops Foster, several bass players.

ctx.x: So, um, I did, uh, record that Roy Palmer I got on trombone and later Kid Ory on trombone. And, uh, um, St. Cyr, of course, and Pops Foster, several bass players. Uh, uh, Ed Garland, Montuti, they call it. He was one of my very favorite musicians. He still plays in California. Well, anyway, I have about 20 interviews, uh, different instruments. Natty Dominic, um, on trumpet. Bunk would have been a logical one. He was already dead. I never did get Louie. I would have tried to get him sometime, although it's a…
And this is on the New Orleans Ensemble Stock.

items.q: I know it was either Ori or Bud Scott. I don't remember which one. It could have been Mutt Carey.

ctx.x: Well, how important was the religious feeling in influencing all of this? Well, I think that's difficult to say, too.

Of course, for people like me that came down here years after it started, I would never know. But other people like, say, Kid Ori, for instance, and some of the first people I met in California, like Bud Scott, one of the old-timers, quite a few of those said that a lot of the music came right out of the churches of the jazz bands as if... I know it was either Ori or Bud Scott. I don't remember which one. It could have been Mutt Carey. I'm talking about Buddy Bolden. They said, well, he got all of his music right…
What about the street marches, the funeral marches? Are they all the same thing?
